Topic: If virtue is meant to be the same for all rational beings, by what right do we call a woman "virtuous" for her modesty and obedience when we would never praise a man for the same, and who profits from keeping the two measures apart?
Montaigne — Judgement:
I take up the question of whether "virtue" can wear two coats, one cut for women and one for men. I confess I have always found it odd that we praise a woman for a modesty and obedience we would think merely dull, or servile, in a man.

If virtue is a single thing, a firm and constant disposition of the soul, then a virtue that depends on the sex of its bearer is not virtue at all but custom with a halo on it. I have said that women are not so far from men: in understanding and in the capacity for friendship, the difference lies mostly in education and in the liberty we allow them. So who profits from the double measure? We do, we men, who want a household quiet and a lineage certain, and who have dressed our convenience in the language of the soul. Obedience praised in one sex and not the other is simply a leash we have been calling a jewel.

My verdict: the praise of a woman for modesty and obedience is a flattery of the master's comfort, and true virtue, whose measure is courage, justice, and temperance, is the same in her as in him.

*Call it virtue only if you would praise it in yourself; otherwise it is a leash with a ribbon on it.*
Austen — Judgement:
I take this to be a question of bookkeeping: why do we enter a woman's virtue in one ledger and a man's in another, when Reason, if it is one, keeps a single account?

A woman is praised for modesty and obedience because she has little else to bring to market. With no profession, no inheritance and no vote, her agreeableness is her only capital, and Charlotte Lucas accepts Mr. Collins because such "virtue" is the price of bread. Those who profit are fathers, husbands and heirs of entailed estates, who find an obliging dependant cheaper than an equal, and who then mistake her necessity for her nature.

We have no right whatever: what we call female virtue is dependence flattered into merit, and it serves the men who hold the estate.

*Praise a woman for her obedience and you have only thanked her for her poverty.*
Bashō — Judgement:
You ask whether virtue is one thing or two, and I hear the old lesson of pine and bamboo: do we ask the plant what it is, or only the gardener who prunes it?

I was taught to learn of the pine from the pine, and of the bamboo from the bamboo, meaning we should attend to the thing itself, not the shape imposed on it. Modesty and obedience are praised in a woman and go unremarked in a man. They are not her nature but a trellis, built for the comfort of fathers, husbands and households, who gain a quiet voice and a ready meal. Virtue that must be commanded, and of only half the world, is mere convenience in virtue's robe.

There is one virtue, honest presence to the moment before us, and any praise that bends by sex is flattery paid to whoever profits.

*A virtue with two measures is a debt, and the one who collects is never the one who pays.*
Emerson — Judgement:
Virtue, I hold, is not a livery cut to the wearer's station but the one law of the soul, and to praise in woman a modesty and obedience we would scorn in man is to confess that we are praising a habit and calling it a character.

What is really at stake is self-trust. "Whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist," I wrote, and the sentence has no second clause for women; obedience to custom, to the voice outside, is precisely the surrender of the divine within, whoever surrenders it. The double measure profits those who find a soul that defers more convenient than a soul that decides: it feeds the comfort of the household tyrant and the timid vanity of the society that wishes to be flattered by conformity. I have said that the sphere of woman is whatever her genius assigns her, and no usage may fence it in beforehand.

Modesty that springs from reverence for one's own nature is a virtue in either sex; obedience to another's will is a virtue in neither, and we have no right to praise in women what we despise in men.

*A virtue that needs a second price-tag was never virtue, only service dressed in praise.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
I take the question as one of rights, not manners: a virtue that bends to the sex of its bearer is no virtue at all, but a livery, cut to the wearer's station and stitched by those who gain by it.

Modesty and obedience are not moral qualities; they are the habits of the dependent. We praise them in women as we praise them in subjects, because a creature who is trained to yield never learns to claim. Mary Wollstonecraft saw it plainly: you cannot deny a being education and property, then applaud her for the weakness you have manufactured. The profit falls to those who hold the pen, the purse and the vote, for whom a pliant half of mankind is cheaper than a free one, as the hereditary throne is cheaper than a republic of equals.

Virtue is single, and any measure that gives one standard to men and another to women is a monarchy in the household, to be abolished as I would abolish the other.

*Where the same act earns praise in one sex and reproach in the other, you have found not a virtue but a master.*
Keynes — Judgement:
Virtue, if it is a quality of rational beings, cannot carry a sex; yet we have made modesty and obedience a woman's whole character, and praise her for the very qualities that cost her nothing in power and us nothing in comfort. I am less a moralist than a student of who gains from conventions that are called natural.

The double measure is no accident of manners. It is a settled arrangement, like the old faith in thrift for its own sake, which kept wealth idle while we told ourselves that restraint was a virtue. Obedience praised in one half of the population is a labour and an influence that society neither pays for nor puts to use. Whoever holds the household purse, the vote and the profession profits from the other's "virtue", and so lets the convention pass for nature. I have seen economies ruin themselves by wasting productive capacity, and a polity that leaves half its judgement unused does the same.

We have no right to call modesty and obedience virtues in women when we would not praise them in men, and the men and institutions that profit from the habit have every reason to keep it.

*A virtue that benefits only the person who praises it is not a virtue but a tariff.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
By what right? By none that survives the impartial spectator's gaze. I take the question to be whether praise tracks genuine virtue or merely tracks convenience, and I observe that we have two ledgers of "virtue" kept in one household.

When I wrote of the sentiments, I held that approbation is earned by conduct an impartial spectator can sympathise with, and that self-command is the master virtue of both sexes. Yet custom taught that a man's honour lay in courage and a woman's in chastity and compliance, and I noted in the *Theory of Moral Sentiments* how fashion bends our very sense of the praiseworthy. Modesty is a real grace in any person; but obedience prized as the whole of a woman's merit is not virtue at all, only the habit of the dependent. Those who profit are plain enough: the head of the household who wants a docile servant, and the guardians of an order that educates half of mankind to please rather than to judge.

A virtue that is praised in one sex only is not virtue but usefulness wearing virtue's coat.

*Where we praise in the weak what we would despise in the strong, we are flattering our own convenience, not honouring their character.*
